share_verdict: Ash gourd held this dish together before the potato did.

source.author: Someśvara III
source.locus: Annabhoga, the rice and vegetable preparations

ingredients.name: ash gourd
ingredients.function: the main vegetable, indigenous to India, high in water, low in starch

ingredients.name: brinjal, bottle gourd, snake gourd, pumpkin, yam
ingredients.function: the everyday vegetables of the period, all of which the potato later displaced

ingredients.name: rice
ingredients.function: the grain, in a supporting rather than dominant role

method_reconstructed: Fry the seasonal vegetables in sesame oil or ghee.
Add rice and water and cook together.
Season with cracked pepper and ginger; sour with tamarind where the region does so.
contested_points: The Mānasollāsa describes numerous rice-and-vegetable preparations rather than one dish called tahiri; mapping the modern name onto them is a convenience, not a continuity claim.

changed.from: ash gourd and other indigenous vegetables, brinjal, bottle gourd, snake gourd, pumpkin, yam
changed.to: potato as the primary bulk vegetable
changed.driver: the potato arrived from the Americas and proved cheaper, more storable and more filling than the gourds and yams it replaced. It did not add a vegetable to the repertoire so much as take over the role several native ones had held

changed.from: tamarind as the sour, pepper and ginger as the heat
changed.to: tomato and/or curd, red and green chilli
changed.driver: both tomato and chilli are Columbian-exchange arrivals

ingredients: 2 cups ash gourd (petha / kumbalanga), diced, or pumpkin, bottle gourd, yam
steps: Fry the diced gourd in sesame oil until the edges colour.
Add the rinsed rice and two and a half cups of water.
Season with cracked pepper and ginger, and a little tamarind water.
Cover and cook until the rice is done and the gourd has collapsed into it.
Lighter and wetter than a potato tahiri, with more of the pot tasting of vegetable than of starch.

verification.note: Transcribed from the editorial extraction, which points at the Mānasollāsa's rice-and-vegetable preparations generally rather than a single passage. Classed RECONSTRUCTED for that reason.
